nodes.content: Determine identifiability of population treatment-policy effects under network interference when treatment influences which social ties are observed.
requirements: Establish identification boundaries under explicit restrictions on interference and treatment-dependent missing ties.
Within identifiable regimes, achieve ≥93% coverage for 95% intervals, with median width ≤2× complete-network oracle.

nodes.content: Under randomized assignment, one-hop interference, and positive treatment-stratified dyad audits, use policy g-computation with cluster-bootstrap intervals and MNAR bounds.
Can positive dyad audits identify one-hop exposure distributions when treatment-dependent reporting also depends on unobserved tie status?
Independent, positive-probability dyad verification enables audit-weighted complete-ego g-computation despite tie-status-dependent reporting.
Simulate 1,000 datasets of 300 eight-person clusters with 90% independent dyad audits and treatment-by-tie reporting; assess coverage and oracle-width ratios.
Across 1,000 simulated datasets, audit-weighted estimates achieved 94.1% coverage, with median interval width 1.6× the complete-network oracle.
Adopt audit-weighted g-computation with independent dyad audits, given 94.1% coverage and 1.6× oracle width; defer unaudited MNAR settings.
Derive complete-ego audit identification and unaudited MNAR counterexamples; test 70–90% audit rates for ≥93% coverage and ≤2× oracle width.
Construct observationally equivalent unaudited MNAR counterexamples; simulate audit-weighted coverage and oracle-width ratios at 70%, 80%, and 90% verification.
AuditBound-v1 report documents complete-ego identification, observationally equivalent unaudited MNAR models, and coverage/oracle-width tables at 70%, 80%, and 90% verification.
Audit AuditBound-v1 derivations and reanalyze its 70–90% verification tables against ≥93% coverage and ≤2× oracle width.
AuditBound-v1 confirms audited identification and unaudited MNAR nonidentification; at 80–90% audits, coverage reached 93.4–94.1% with 1.8–1.6× oracle width.
Stress-test audit-weighted g-computation across 1,000 datasets with unrecorded degree-dependent audits and two-hop spillovers; measure coverage and oracle-width ratios.
With one-hop interference and 80% treatment-stratified audit positivity, unrecorded degree-dependent verification reduced coverage to 87.2% (1.8× oracle width).
Retain one-hop audit-weighted inference with independent dyad verification; exclude unrecorded degree-dependent audits after coverage fell to 87.2%.
Randomly census 80% of isolated clusters; use design-weighted g-computation under assignment positivity to allow arbitrary within-cluster interference.
Can 80% cluster censuses deliver precise policy intervals when arbitrary interference makes relevant treatment vectors rare?
For eight-person isolated clusters, 80% random censuses and policy-to-randomization likelihood ratios ≤3 yield ≥93% coverage and ≤2× oracle width.
Simulate 1,000 datasets with 300 eight-person clusters, treatment-dependent tie reporting, 80% random censuses, and policy ratios ≤3; measure coverage/oracle-width.
Across 1,000 simulated datasets, 80% random cluster censuses yielded 94.0% coverage and 1.7× oracle width under policy ratios ≤3.
Stress-test 80% random cluster censuses across 1,000 eight-person-cluster datasets with rare bridge-tie spillovers and policy ratios ≤3.
Within isolated eight-person clusters, rare bridge-tie spillovers yielded 89.8% coverage despite 80% random censuses and policy ratios ≤3.
Retain census inference for baseline regimes (94.0% coverage), but defer rare-bridge settings (89.8%) pending bridge-aware intervals.
With ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters, bridge-stratified bootstrap intervals restore ≥93% coverage and ≤2× oracle width under policy ratios ≤3.
Simulate 1,000 300-cluster datasets with ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters, 80% census, ratios ≤3; assess bridge-stratified bootstrap coverage/oracle-width.
Across 1,000 simulations with ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters, stratified bootstrap coverage reached 93.6%, with median width 1.9× oracle.
Extend census inference to rare-bridge regimes only with ≥20 bridge-positive censused clusters and stratified bootstrap (93.6% coverage; 1.9× oracle width).
Recover one-hop exposure distributions from three conditionally independent treatment-stratified tie reporters with zero false positives, then bootstrap policy g-computation.
Does latent degree-driven dependence among tie reporters invalidate exposure identification despite treatment-stratified three-reporter agreement?
Latent degree-driven reporter dependence permits observationally equivalent tie distributions with policy effects differing by ≥0.05, defeating three-reporter identification.
Construct observationally equivalent degree-dependent three-reporter models and test whether their one-hop policy effects differ by ≥0.05.
Across all latent-degree models under network-independent Bernoulli policies, effect gaps were zero; zero-sensitivity treatment strata defeated three-reporter identification.
Reject unrestricted three-reporter inference because zero-sensitivity strata defeat identification; latent-degree dependence alone did not separate Bernoulli-policy effects.
Randomize isolated clusters 1:1 between Bernoulli(0.3) and Bernoulli(0.7) policies; use cluster-mean contrasts regardless of treatment-dependent tie reporting.
With unequal cluster sizes, does the unweighted cluster-mean contrast identify a cluster-average rather than the population individual-average policy effect?
With unequal cluster sizes, unweighted contrasts identify cluster-average effects; size-weighted contrasts identify individual-average effects under fixed cluster sizes.
Simulate 1,000 unequal-size cluster trials with treatment-dependent tie reporting; compare unweighted versus size-weighted individual-average bias, coverage, and oracle-width.
Across 1,000 unequal-size trials, unweighted individual-effect bias was 0.025; size-weighted coverage reached 94.3% with 1.0× oracle width.
Stress-test size-weighted contrasts across 1,000 trials of 200 isolated clusters (sizes 2–40) with size-correlated effects; assess coverage/oracle-width.
With size-biased cluster enrollment and size-correlated effects, size-weighted contrasts had 0.031 population bias and 87.6% coverage despite fixed sizes.
Use size-weighted policy contrasts only for representative cluster samples; size-biased enrollment requires inverse-inclusion weights after coverage dropped to 87.6%.
With known positive cluster-inclusion probabilities, inverse-inclusion-and-size-weighted contrasts recover individual-average effects at ≥93% coverage despite size-biased enrollment.
Simulate fixed-size clusters under representative versus size-biased enrollment; compare size-weighted contrasts against sample and population individual-average effects.
With fixed sizes, size-weighted contrasts identified sampled individuals’ effects in both designs; population bias appeared only under size-biased enrollment.
Simulate 1,000 size-biased 200-cluster trials (sizes 2–40); assess inverse-inclusion-and-size-weighted population-effect bias, 95% coverage, and oracle-width ratios.
Across 1,000 trials with known positive inclusion probabilities, extreme enrollment weights yielded 89.1% coverage and 2.3× oracle width.
Rerun 1,000 size-biased trials with inclusion-probability ratios ≤4; assess inverse-inclusion-and-size-weighted coverage, oracle-width, and effective sample size.
With inclusion-probability ratios ≤4, inverse-inclusion-and-size weighting achieved 94.0% coverage, 1.5× oracle width, and median effective sample size 164.
For size-biased population effects, adopt inverse-inclusion-and-size weighting only with inclusion-probability ratios ≤4; extreme weights missed both targets.
Prove randomized isolated-cluster identification despite treatment-dependent missing ties; benchmark ratio-≤4 inclusion weighting against ≥93% coverage and ≤2× oracle width.
Derive design-weighted identification under arbitrary within-cluster interference and treatment-dependent tie reporting; benchmark ratio-≤4 enrollment weights over 1,000 trials.
PolicyTrial-v1 contains isolated-cluster identification proof, inverse-inclusion-and-size-weighted estimator, and 1,000-trial coverage/oracle-width benchmarks for inclusion ratios ≤4.
Audit PolicyTrial-v1 proof and rerun its 1,000-trial ratio-≤4 benchmarks; assess population-effect bias, coverage, and oracle-width.
PolicyTrial-v1 audit confirmed identification despite treatment-dependent tie reporting; ratio-≤4 weighted trials achieved 94.0% coverage and 1.5× oracle width.
Prioritize ratio-≤4 isolated-cluster trials (94% coverage; 1.5× oracle width); retain audited one-hop and bridge-stratified census alternatives, reject unrestricted three-reporters.
